title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front - Nature Astronomy
byline: Davis; Hillary; Bland-Hawthorn; Joss; Tepper-García; Thor; Agertz; Oscar; Iles; Elizabeth J
html:
Abstract

The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Norma–outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the ‘Norma arm’ extending from one end of the Galaxy’s central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. Here we use a new generation of N-body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year-old masers instead trace the Galactic bar’s quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the parameters of the bar to be: a ≈ 4.3 ± 0.2 kpc, b ≈ 2.3 ± 0.2 kpc, ϕ = \({{20}_{-2}^{+5}}^{\circ }\) and Ωp ≲ 40 km s−1 kpc−1, representing the semimajor and semiminor half-lengths of the bar, the inclination angle and the pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way’s spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

Main

Maser observations from the BeSSeL Survey and Japanese VERA project have previously been used to trace the ‘Norma arm’ at its location near the Galactic bar end, beginning at (x, y) ≈ (−2, 3) kpc and curving anticlockwise to approximately (−4, 0) kpc (ref. 1), where x and y are galactocentric coordinates with the Sun at (−8.5, 0). In some interpretations, the Norma arm continues around to the far side of the Galactic Centre, connecting with the outer arm to form the so-called Norma–outer arm (see Fig. 1 of ref. 1 for a schematic of the various spiral-arm locations). However, recent work suggests that some of the young stars traditionally attributed to Norma actually reside on x1 orbits of the Galactic bar, in which case the arm terminates at the end of the bar2.

Gas structures in the bar region are commonly understood with reference to x1 and x2 orbits (Extended Data Fig. 1). Gas flows inwards along the x1 orbit family, eventually reaching an innermost ‘cusped’ x1 orbit3,4. At smaller radii, oval-shaped x2 orbits appear. The pericentre of the cusped x1 orbit grazes the apocentre of the outermost x2 orbits, causing shocks to occur3,4,5,6, which drive gas inwards to the x2 family.

In the bar region of the Milky Way (MW), several key structures appear in the gas: (1) a nuclear disk or ring or central molecular zone, which is a dense ring of molecular gas on x2 orbits4,7,8,9, (2) two distinct dust lanes or connecting arms, which we argue follow bar-generated shock fronts along the outer edges of the bar, and (3) a gas-poor ‘shock cavity’ along the bar between the dust lanes and the nuclear disk10. These features of the MW gas distribution are seen in stellar bars of external galaxies: for example NGC 1433 observed with the James Webb Space telescope (available at https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/ngc-1433-miri-image).

In the local Universe, star formation (SF) is often suppressed along stellar bars (for example NGC 3351, 1512, 4303 and 5383)5,6,11,12,13,14,15. Specifically, SF is often low along the bar dust lanes between the nuclear disk and bar ends, despite their substantial reservoirs of dense gas16,17,18. This has been explained by several mechanisms, including bar torques that funnel gas inwards, starving the dust lanes of gas needed for SF19,20,21,22, or bar-driven shocks and shear, which inhibit the growth of gravitational instabilities by driving turbulence6,13,23.

However, the suppression of SF along local bars is not universal. NGC 7479, NGC 3359, NGC 2903 and NGC 1503, for example, all exhibit notable SF along their dust lanes, probably due to, respectively: a recent minor merger, ample gas supply in a young bar, a broken feathery dust lane structure that weakens the shear and shocks, and stars forming in dust spurs but later migrating to dust lanes16,24,25,26,27,28,29.

Furthermore, whether the Galactic bar is long and slow (bar half-length Rb ≈ 5 kpc and pattern speed Ωp ≈ 35–45 km s−1 kpc−1)30,31,32 or short and fast (Rb ≈ 3.5 kpc and Ωp ≈ 50–60 km s−1 kpc−1)33,34,35,36,37 remains highly debated. Many of the bar properties proposed in the literature are based on observations of MW gas in Galactic longitude and line-of-sight velocity (ℓ, Vlos) space3,7,10,38,39,40,41 (for example, Extended Data Fig. 2).

The (ℓ, Vlos) diagrams, formed by the superposition of structures along lines of sight, cannot be deprojected into a unique (x, y, z, vx, vy, vz) distribution. For pure circular motion, the tangent-point (TP) circle in (x, y) maps perfectly to the terminal velocity curve in (ℓ, Vlos) (Extended Data Fig. 3). For gas on circular orbits about the Galactic Centre, each orbit within the solar circle has two points where a line of sight from the Sun is tangent to the orbit (one each at ℓ > 0 and ℓ < 0). The TP circle is defined as the locus of these points, forming a circle that connects the Sun and the Galactic Centre. Additionally, the terminal velocity curve is the outer envelope of an (ℓ, Vlos) diagram, that is the maximum ∣Vlos∣ for each longitude (Extended Data Fig. 3). However, in real galaxies, non-circular motions break this one-to-one correspondence between the TP circle and terminal curve.

There are numerous flaws with the current interpretation of gas features related to bars and spirals in (ℓ, Vlos) diagrams. In the following, Galactic quadrants I and IV are defined by 0° < ℓ < 90° and −90° < ℓ < 0°, respectively, with the Sun at (−8.5, 0) kpc (Fig. 1). In (ℓ, Vlos) space, the quadrant I connecting arm or dust lane is identified as a ridge (also labelled in Extended Data Fig. 2), which begins at the maximum Vlos for ℓ > 0, then decreases continuously in Vlos while increasing continuously in ℓ, before ending near ℓ ≈ 10°, where gas is sparse7,42. This connecting arm (ℓ, Vlos) requires a bar that: (1) has a straight quadrant I dust lane, as only a straight lane can increase monotonically in longitude as we move away from the nuclear disk (a curved lane would eventually decrease in ℓ as it wraps around the bar; Extended Data Fig. 4), (2) hosts a very compact nuclear ring (−1° ≲ ℓ ≲ 1. 5°, R ≈ 0.23 kpc predicted by TP methods, R = R0 sin ℓ, where R is the tangent-point radius and R0 is the solar radius), (3) is short enough overall to remain confined to ∣ℓ∣ ≲ 10° and (4) has a gas-poor bar end, as the connecting arm (ℓ, Vlos) ridge terminates at a zone very deficient in gas. This is inconsistent with the standard picture of bars, in which bar ends are gas-rich and often star-forming and with gas being funnelled inwards along the bar dust lanes. We, instead, propose that the bar dust lanes lie at larger radii, intersecting the terminal curve near ∣ℓ∣ ≈ 20°, a region traditionally attributed to spiral arms.

Top left: stellar density distribution at t = 3.95 Gyr in the model. The bar has been oriented at 25° relative to the x axis. Galactic quadrants I (0° < ℓ < 90°) and IV (−90° < ℓ < 0°) are labelled. The white dashed lines represent several key lines of longitude ℓ = 0°, ±30°, ±90° and 180°. The white dashed circle marks the location of the TP circle. Top right: the corresponding gas density distribution. The cyan dashed lines mark the approximate imprint of the stellar bar on the gas distribution. Bottom left: KD error map. Red diamond-like features in this panel result from gas that has been omitted because it does not meet the requirements of the kinematic distance method. Bottom right: the low KD error zones (∣(dk − dtrue)/dtrue∣ < 0.02) are shown in green. The white scatter point with black outline at (x, y) = (−8.5, 0) kpc represents the Sun. The black contours overlaid on all panels are stellar density contours, taken from the top left stellar density distribution.

In this work, we argue that masers, typically linked to regions of massive SF, align with the dust lane in the Galactic bar in quadrant I. We focus on an N-body, hydrodynamical model that is designed to reproduce the MW as much as possible (model 1)10,43 (Methods). Masers result from a population inversion in molecular energy levels, where stimulated emission produces the coherent amplification of radiation at appropriate microwave or radio frequencies44,45,46.

From the match between the Norma masers and the simulated bar shock front in both (x, y) space and (ℓ, Vlos) space, (1) we identified a curved dust lane, (2) we found that SF is not fully suppressed in the bar region, (3) we argue that the Norma arm is not a spiral arm but a shock front along the Galactic bar and (4) we estimated the bar properties to be abar ≈ 4.3 ± 0.2 kpc, bbar ≈ 2.3 ± 0.2 kpc and \(\phi ={{20}_{-2}^{+5}}^{\circ }\).

We begin by applying the kinematic distance (KD) method to our MW ‘surrogate’ simulation and using low KD error zones to isolate gas near the bar shock fronts (sections ‘Kinematic error maps’ and ‘Low KD error zone along bar shock front’). Next, we identify a distinct feature observed in CO diagrams, which we call the ‘second peak’ (Extended Data Fig. 2), and relate this to the longitude where the TP circle and bar dust lane intersect (section ‘The second peak’). This result is reproduced in a second simulation (section ‘Comparison with a second simulation’). Finally, the simulated shock front is matched with the location of Norma masers in both (x, y) space and (ℓ, Vlos) space. This is used to constrain the size and orientation of the bar (section ‘Constraining the Galactic bar size and angle’) and to suggest that the dust lane in the Galactic bar is star-forming (section ‘SF in the bar’).

Kinematic error maps

The KD method estimates the distance of a gas cloud from the Sun using its Galactic longitude ℓ and line-of-sight velocity Vlos and by assuming circular motion. See section ‘KD method’ in Methods for details.

Figure 1 (bottom left) shows a basic map of the KD error, (dk − dtrue)/dtrue, for our model at t = 3.95 Gyr. Here dk is the KD estimate, and dtrue is the actual heliocentric distance taken from the simulation. To put these results into context, the first row of Fig. 1 displays a stellar density projection (left) and a gas density projection (right) for our simulation at the same time. The model features a stellar bar, which we have oriented at a 25° angle relative to the x = 0 axis. In the bottom right corner of Fig. 1, we isolate zones of low KD error (∣(dk − dtrue)/dtrue∣ < 0.02) in green.

Low KD error zone along bar shock front

In the gas density projection (Fig. 1, top right), the bar shock fronts, or dust lanes, are labelled. These dense structures occur along the leading sides of the bar, where inflowing gas is compressed by bar-driven shocks.

In Fig. 2, we zoom in on low KD error zones in the bar region (left), and map these points into (ℓ, Vlos) space (right). The low KD error zone adjacent to the leading edge of the bar and nuclear spiral in quadrant I (presented with the magma, or dark purple to pale yellow, colour map) appears as a loop-like structure at ℓ > 0 in (ℓ, Vlos). The magma-coloured points in (ℓ, Vlos) exhibit a clear peak, which is labelled the second peak in Fig. 2, and it maps to an intersection point between the TP circle and the bar dust lane (lime green points).

Gas density distributions in (x, y) space (left) and (ℓ, Vlos) space (right) at t = 3.95 Gyr in the model. We isolate low KD error zones approximately within the bar region using the white ellipse (drawn by eye), and for the most part, these points are presented in green. However, for the low KD error zone along the leading edge of the bar and the nuclear spiral in quadrant I, a focus of our work, we colour these with a magma colour map (dark purple to pale yellow). This structure is pale yellow near the bar end and then progresses to dark purple as we move towards the bar centre, which allows us to easily visualize the corresponding location of individual points in (ℓ, Vlos) space. The first and second peaks in quadrant I of this simulated (ℓ, Vlos) distribution are labelled. In (x, y), the TP circle and some key lines of longitude are given by the white dashed circle and white dashed lines, respectively. We emphasize that the intersection of the TP circle with the bar dust lane occurs at the location of the second peak in (ℓ, Vlos) (lime green points).

The second peak

Extended Data Fig. 2 presents the (ℓ, Vlos) distribution of carbon monoxide (CO) observed in the MW. We label the first and second peaks in quadrant I (0° < ℓ < 90°). These are defined as a sharp change in ∣Vlos∣ along the terminal velocity curve, such that we can identify an obvious visual peak. In quadrant IV (−90° < ℓ < 0°), three analogous ‘peak-like’ features are also present but are not the focus of this work. A more detailed definition of the peaks is given in ‘Identifying peaks in simulated (ℓ, Vlos) distributions’ in Methods.

Figure 3 compares Vlos along the TP circle (magenta curves) with the outer envelope of simulated (ℓ, Vlos) diagrams (grey distributions). This analysis was performed for all barred snapshots in our MW surrogate model. Results for representative times between t = 1.44 Gyr and 3.95 Gyr are shown. See section ‘Vlos around the TP circle’ in Methods for details.

Simulated (ℓ, Vlos) gas distributions (shown in grey) for our MW surrogate simulation for selected snapshots between t = 1.44 Gyr and 3.95 Gyr. Blue points mark the true first and second peaks. Occasionally, a third peak is marked as well. The magenta curves show the mean Vlos and ℓ values computed around the TP circle (see section ‘Vlos around the TP circle’ in Methods for details). Overall, the magenta curves have a very similar shape to the outer envelope of the corresponding grey (ℓ, Vlos) distributions.

summary: The Norma spiral arm reveals that stars can form under very diverse conditions in the Universe.
